justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It points at the else branch evaluating `handleOrId.refresh` and says this "throws a TypeError" when the native timer "returns undefined or null". It also notes the old code explicitly guarded against a nullish handle. This is the same code and the same failure mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: In `patchTimer`'s `scheduleTask`, the change stores the native timer's return value in `handleOrId`. When it is not a number, it executes `data.isRefreshable = isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)`. Some environments return null or undefined from `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`requestAnimationFrame`, for example a browser extension, policy or automation wrapper that blocks the call. The old code explicitly tolerated a nullish handle. With this change, reading `.refresh` on null throws a TypeError synchronously, so calling the patched `setTimeout` crashes instead of returning. The fix uses optional chaining (`handleOrId?.refresh`) so a nullish handle is treated as non-refreshable.

findings.description: If the native setTimeout/setInterval/setImmediate/requestAnimationFrame returns undefined or null, `isNumber` is false and the else branch evaluates `handleOrId.refresh`, which throws a TypeError. The old code explicitly guarded against this case with 'check whether handle is null, because some polyfill or browser may return undefined'. The same crash applies to any non-numeric, non-object return value. Scheduling the timer now throws instead of returning the task.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It points out that `handleOrId.refresh` is read without a guard when the handle is not a number, and that this throws a TypeError when setTimeout and similar calls return null or undefined. That is the same defect and the same mechanism as the known bug. Finding 1 is about the removed ref/unref copying, which is a different issue.
ground_truth: In `patchTimer`'s `scheduleTask`, the change stores the native timer's return value in `handleOrId`. When it is not a number, it executes `data.isRefreshable = isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)`. Some environments return null or undefined from `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`requestAnimationFrame`, for example a browser extension, policy or automation wrapper that blocks the call. The old code explicitly tolerated a nullish handle. With this change, reading `.refresh` on null throws a TypeError synchronously, so calling the patched `setTimeout` crashes instead of returning. The fix uses optional chaining (`handleOrId?.refresh`) so a nullish handle is treated as non-refreshable.

findings.description: When the native set function returns a non-number, the code reads `handleOrId.refresh` unguarded. Some polyfills and browsers return `undefined` or `null` from setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate or requestAnimationFrame, and the old code explicitly handled that. In those cases this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'refresh')` while scheduling, which is a regression.

The code that copied `handle.ref` and `handle.unref` onto the task (`task.ref` and `task.unref`) was removed. When a task is returned in place of the handle (non-Node or polyfilled environments), callers lose `ref`/`unref` support. This is an unrelated behaviour regression.

justification: The only finding, [0], is about a comment typo where "idents" was changed to "indents". The known bug is different: the `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/` match in `_applySelectorScope` drops everything after a newline in selector parts that now contain parenthesized content. Finding [0] does not touch on that behavior.
ground_truth: In `ShadowCss._scopeSelector`/`_applySelectorScope`, the change replaced the simple `/ ?, ?/` comma split and the combinator separator with regexes that do not split inside parentheses. A selector part like `.foo:is(.a,\n.b)` therefore now reaches `_scopeSelectorPart` as a single string that can contain newlines. That function splits the part with `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/`, both in the newly added pseudo-function `:host` branch (`scopedP.match(...)`) and in the non-host branch (`t.match(...)`). Because `.` does not match a newline, everything after the first newline is silently dropped. For example, a component style `.foo:is(.a,\n.b) {}` is emitted as `.foo[contenta]:is(.a,`, with the rest of the selector and the closing parenthesis lost, which breaks the stylesheet. The fix changed the trailing group of both regexes to `([\s\S]*)` so content after newlines is kept.

findings.description: The comment edit changes "idents" to "indents". The regex documentation describes valid CSS identifiers, so "indents" is a wrong term and makes the comment misleading. Runtime behavior is not affected.

justification: Finding 1 matches part of the known bug. It says `init()` "is now called inside `afterRenderEffect`, which re-runs on every `componentExplorerView` update. Each run registers another `highlightComponent` listener ... and recreate both visualizers." The ground truth names this same defect, and the fix addresses it by calling `init()` only once. Finding 0 is about unused sorting, which is a different issue. Finding 2's main claim is that author `:host` display styles override `[hidden]`, which is a different mechanism. It does mention losing the `visibility:hidden` layout case, but it never ties this to the effect running D3 layout while the tree is hidden.
ground_truth: This change rewrites `InjectorTreeComponent` to render from an `afterRenderEffect` that runs whenever the `componentExplorerView` input changes. The effect calls `init()` and `updateInjectorTreeVisualization(view.forest)` without checking whether the tab is visible. The change also hides the deferred `ng-injector-tree` with `[hidden]` (display:none) and removes the old `ng-injector- tree.hidden` CSS, which had kept the element laid out with `visibility: hidden`. So once the Injector Tree tab has been opened and the user switches to another tab, every new component explorer view re-runs the effect. D3 then tries to lay out, translate and snap SVG trees inside an element with no layout, which throws errors. `init()` also runs on every effect execution, re-registering the `highlightComponent` listener and recreating the visualizers each time. The fix adds a `hidden` input bound to the host's `[hidden]`, returns early from the effect when it is true (read untracked), and calls `init()` only once, when the visualizers do not exist yet.

findings.description: The template still passes `providers()` to `ng-injector-providers`, not the new `sortedProviders()`. The sorting that used to run when `latestInjectorProviders` arrived was removed from the message handler and moved into `sortedProviders`, which nothing uses. The providers list now shows in the order the backend sends it, which regresses the previous alphabetical-by-token order.

`init()` is now called inside `afterRenderEffect`, which re-runs on every `componentExplorerView` update. Each run registers another `highlightComponent` listener, so handlers accumulate and fire multiple times per message. Each run also calls `setUpEnvironmentInjectorVisualizer` and `setUpElementInjectorVisualizer`, which clean up and recreate both visualizers. This resets the user's zoom, pan and selection on every refresh, and `init()` previously ran only once.

Tab visibility was switched from a `display:none` CSS class to the `[hidden]` attribute on component host elements, and the `.hidden` rules were deleted. The `hidden` attribute only applies the UA default `display:none`. Any author style such as `:host {display:block/flex}` on these components overrides it, so inactive tabs can stay visible and stack on screen. The previous `ng-injector-tree.hidden` special case, which used `visibility:hidden` and absolute positioning so the tree could still be laid out and measured, is also gone.

justification:
Finding 0 matches. It points at the same faulty code: the `afterRenderEffect` that calls `init()` on every `componentExplorerView` change. It describes part of the known bug's mechanism: "Each call registers another `highlightComponent` message-bus listener... It also recreates both `InjectorTreeVisualizer`s each time." The known bug lists exactly this, and the fix makes `init()` run only once.

Finding 1 does not match. It is about the unused `sortedProviders`, which is a different issue.

Finding 2 does not match. Its main claim is that author `display` styles override `[hidden]`, so inactive tabs may stay visible. That is a different mechanism. It briefly notes that the CSS keeping the SVG "measurable while hidden" was removed. However, it never links this to the effect re-running while the tab is hidden and causing D3 layout errors.

The effect calls `init()` and `updateInjectorTreeVisualization(view.forest)` without checking whether the tab is visible. The change also hides the deferred `ng-injector-tree` with `[hidden]` (display:none) and removes the old `ng-injector- tree.hidden` CSS, which had kept the element laid out with `visibility: hidden`. So once the Injector Tree tab has been opened and the user switches to another tab, every new component explorer view re-runs the effect. D3 then tries to lay out, translate and snap SVG trees inside an element with no layout, which throws errors. `init()` also runs on every effect execution, re-registering the `highlightComponent` listener and recreating the visualizers each time. The fix adds a `hidden` input bound to the host's `[hidden]`, returns early from the effect when it is true (read untracked), and calls `init()` only once, when the visualizers do not exist yet.

findings.description: `init()` is called inside `afterRenderEffect` on every `componentExplorerView` change. Each call registers another `highlightComponent` message-bus listener, so listeners accumulate and fire repeatedly. It also recreates both `InjectorTreeVisualizer`s each time, which discards the user's pan/zoom state and rebuilds the graph on every update. Previously the listeners were registered once and the visualizers were created once.

The template still passes the raw `providers()` to `ng-injector-providers` and checks `providers().length`. The new `sortedProviders` computed is never used, so the provider list is no longer sorted by token. This regresses the previous behavior, where providers were sorted before being set.

Tab visibility now relies on the `[hidden]` attribute instead of the `.hidden` class with `display:none`. The attribute only applies the user-agent `display:none`, which any author style such as `:host { display: block/flex }` on these components overrides. Inactive tabs may therefore stay visible and stack on screen. The old `ng-injector-tree.hidden` handling that kept the SVG measurable while hidden was also removed.

justification: Finding 0 flags the same defect. The zone.js label was switched to `//:node_modules/zone.js`, but the shell-browser `index.html` was not updated. It says that if it "still expect[s] the old layout (for example `./npm/node_modules/...`), the extension page will fail to load zone.js". It also notes that `devtools/src/index.html` is unchanged even though devapp now ships zone.js under a different path. That is exactly the known bug in both files, despite the low confidence rating.
ground_truth: The change switches the zone.js dependency in `devtools/src/BUILD.bazel` (the `devapp` pkg_web) and `devtools/projects/shell-browser/src/BUILD.bazel` (the static files filegroup). It goes from `@npm//:node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js` to the workspace target `//:node_modules/zone.js`. That moves the packaged file from `./npm/node_modules/zone.js/...` to `./node_modules/zone.js/...`. The change updated the `<script>` tag only in `demo-standalone/src/index.html`. `devtools/src/index.html` and `devtools/projects/shell-browser/src/index.html` still reference `./npm/node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js`. In both the DevTools dev app and the production browser-extension build, that script 404s and zone.js is never loaded, so the zone-based Angular app fails to bootstrap or run correctly. The fix updated both index.html files to load `./node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js`.

findings.description: The single-file label `@npm//:node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js` was replaced by the whole `//:node_modules/zone.js` package target. The shell-browser `index.html` and any rules that copy or reference `zone.umd.min.js` by path were not updated in this diff. If they still expect the old layout (for example `./npm/node_modules/...`), the extension page will fail to load zone.js. The same applies to `devtools/src/BUILD.bazel`, where `devapp` now ships zone.js under a different path and `tslib.js` is no longer shipped, but `devtools/src/index.html` is unchanged.

findings.description: The devapp now packages zone.js from `//:node_modules/zone.js`, so it lands at `node_modules/zone.js/...`, not the old `npm/node_modules/zone.js/...`. justification: Finding 0 points to the same unguarded `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)[-1]` call on `__` names. It describes the same mechanism: non-field final parts such as a property or method raise an uncaught `FieldDoesNotExist`, so pages that previously rendered via getattr traversal now crash ("the changelist crashes instead of rendering the value"). This matches the known bug.
ground_truth: The change makes `lookup_field()` in `django/contrib/admin/utils.py` call `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)[-1]` unconditionally whenever a `list_display` name contains `__`, so it can render boolean icons for related BooleanFields. Before this, such names were resolved only by walking attributes with `getattr`, which also works for paths whose last part is not a concrete model field, such as a method, a property or `__str__` on a related model. `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` for those paths, and the exception is not caught. Because `lookup_field` is shared by the changelist and readonly-field rendering, entries traversing relations, including second-degree ones (e.g. `book__author__get_full_name` or `parent__parent__some_property`), now crash with an exception where they previously displayed fine. The fix removes this lookup from `lookup_field`. It instead resolves the final field only in `items_for_result` when `f` is None, wrapped in `try/except FieldDoesNotExist`.

findings.description: The new call `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)[-1]` runs for every `__`-separated name resolved by attribute traversal. That includes non-field attributes on the related object, such as a property, method or annotation (e.g. `list_display = ['parent__some_property']`). `get_fields_from_path` resolves each segment with `_meta.get_field`, so it raises `FieldDoesNotExist` (or `NotRelationField`) for those names. `lookup_field` previously returned the value via `getattr` traversal. The exception is raised inside the `except` handler and not caught, so the changelist crashes instead of rendering the value. The call needs a try/except that falls back to `f = None`.

justification: Finding 0 states that the change "adds an unguarded `get_fields_from_path()` call, which can raise NotRelationField or FieldDoesNotExist in cases where the plain getattr traversal worked, such as a path ending in a property or a custom attribute. That would crash the changelist." This is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism as the known bug. The finding also raises an additional FK concern, but the matching part is clearly identified.
ground_truth: The change makes `lookup_field()` in `django/contrib/admin/utils.py` call `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)[-1]` unconditionally whenever a `list_display` name contains `__`, so it can render boolean icons for related BooleanFields. Before this, such names were resolved only by walking attributes with `getattr`, which also works for paths whose last part is not a concrete model field, such as a method, a property or `__str__` on a related model. `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` for those paths, and the exception is not caught. Because `lookup_field` is shared by the changelist and readonly-field rendering, entries traversing relations, including second-degree ones (e.g. `book__author__get_full_name` or `parent__parent__some_property`), now crash with an exception where they previously displayed fine. The fix removes this lookup from `lookup_field`. It instead resolves the final field only in `items_for_result` when `f` is None, wrapped in `try/except FieldDoesNotExist`.

findings.description: lookup_field() now returns the final field `f` for any `a__b` path. Callers such as `items_for_result` treat a non-None `f` as a model field of the row object. For a path ending in a ForeignKey (e.g. `parent__parent`), `f.remote_field` is a ManyToOneRel, so the changelist runs `getattr(result, f.name)` with only the last segment. That returns the wrong object (the row's own `parent`) instead of the traversed value. It also adds an unguarded `get_fields_from_path()` call, which can raise NotRelationField or FieldDoesNotExist in cases where the plain getattr traversal worked, such as a path ending in a property or a custom attribute. That would crash the changelist instead of rendering the value.

justification: Finding 0 is about empty terms becoming None and producing IS NULL matches, plus extra queries for ModelChoiceField. The known bug has two cases: TypedChoiceField.to_python returns the raw string, which causes a ValueError and HTTP 500, and BooleanField.to_python maps arbitrary strings to True. Both stem from to_python not rejecting invalid terms, but the finding describes a different mechanism and different fields.
ground_truth: The change rewrote `ModelAdmin.get_search_results` so that, for non-text `__exact` search fields, each search term is validated with `validate_field.formfield().to_python(bit)`. Lookups whose term raises `ValidationError` are skipped; all others are passed to the ORM with the converted value. This validation does not reject invalid terms for two kinds of fields. First, fields with `choices` produce a `TypedChoiceField`, whose `to_python()` returns the raw string unchanged. So searching "john" against an `IntegerField(choices=...)` with `field__exact` sends "john" to the ORM, which raises `ValueError` and makes the changelist return HTTP 500. Second, `forms.BooleanField.to_python()` maps almost any non-false string to True, so an arbitrary term like "xyz" against `bool__exact` matches every row where the field is True instead of matching nothing. The fix uses `formfield.clean()` for Typed(Multiple)ChoiceField so values are coerced and validated, and uses strict boolean and null-boolean parsers that raise `ValidationError` for unrecognized strings.

findings.description: Converting the term with `formfield.to_python(bit)` can return `None` for an empty term, such as a quoted `""` search. Form fields return `None` for empty values, and `field__exact=None` becomes `IS NULL`. A search for an empty string on an integer, date or similar `__exact` field would then match every row where that field is NULL, instead of skipping the lookup as invalid. Related-field `__exact` lookups also build a `ModelChoiceField` and query the database once per search term, which adds queries.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the BooleanField half of the known bug: `formfield().to_python()` is too permissive. It says "forms.BooleanField.to_python returns True for any string except 'false'..." and that a 'foo' search "matches every True row". That is the same faulty code and mechanism, and it notes that other form fields behave similarly. Finding 1 is about ForeignKey/ModelChoiceField adding extra database queries, which is a different issue.
ground_truth: The change rewrote `ModelAdmin.get_search_results` so that, for non-text `__exact` search fields, each search term is validated with `validate_field.formfield().to_python(bit)`. Lookups whose term raises `ValidationError` are skipped; all others are passed to the ORM with the converted value. This validation does not reject invalid terms for two kinds of fields. First, fields with `choices` produce a `TypedChoiceField`, whose `to_python()` returns the raw string unchanged. So searching "john" against an `IntegerField(choices=...)` with `field__exact` sends "john" to the ORM, which raises `ValueError` and makes the changelist return HTTP 500. Second, `forms.BooleanField.to_python()` maps almost any non-false string to True, so an arbitrary term like "xyz" against `bool__exact` matches every row where the field is True instead of matching nothing. The fix uses `formfield.clean()` for Typed(Multiple)ChoiceField so values are coerced and validated, and uses strict boolean and null-boolean parsers that raise `ValidationError` for unrecognized strings.

findings.description: The search term is converted with `formfield().to_python()`, which is too permissive for some fields. `forms.BooleanField.to_python` returns True for any string except 'false', 'False' and '0'. A `bool__exact` search for 'foo' therefore becomes `bool__exact=True` and matches every True row. Previously the cast-to-string comparison matched nothing. Other form fields that normalise arbitrary input behave the same way. The converted value is also used instead of the raw term, so the query semantics change silently.

When an `fk__exact` search field is used, `prev_field` is the ForeignKey, so `formfield()` is a ModelChoiceField. Its `to_python` runs a database `queryset.get(pk=bit)` for every term and every such lookup during validation. This adds extra queries on every changelist search. The converted value is a model instance that is passed to the filter, and a term that matches no related row is dropped rather than searched. Validation here is meant to be cheap and side-effect free.

justification:
Finding 0 describes the same defect. It says "TextWrapper.wrap() turns '
' into a space and drops it as whitespace, so a blank line returns [] and disappears," and that a trailing newline is lost. It gives the 'a

b' -> 'a
b' example. This is the same mechanism and the same symptoms as the known bug.
ground_truth:
The rewritten `django.utils.text.wrap()` loops over `text.splitlines(True)`, passes each line to `textwrap.TextWrapper.wrap()`, and joins the pieces with "
". `TextWrapper.wrap()` returns an empty list for an empty or whitespace-only line, so those lines vanish from the output. With the default `replace_whitespace=True`, the trailing newline kept by `splitlines(True)` becomes a space and is dropped, so a trailing newline in the input is lost too. For example, `wordwrap("first

second
", 80)` returns "first
second" instead of "first

second
", which merges paragraphs in templates. The fix sets `replace_whitespace=False` and splits with `splitlines()` (no kept ends). It appends the original line whenever the wrapper returns nothing, and appends a final empty element when the text ends with "
".

findings.description:
The rewritten wrap() does not preserve blank lines or trailing newlines. For each line from splitlines(True), TextWrapper.wrap() turns '
' into a space and drops it as whitespace, so a blank line returns [] and disappears. A trailing newline is also stripped by the final '
'.join. As a result, paragraph breaks ('a

b') collapse to 'a
b' and a trailing '
' is lost. This regresses the old behavior of wordwrap and wrap() for existing users.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says each line goes through TextWrapper.wrap, which "turns the newline into a space and then drops it", so a blank line "yields an empty list and disappears". It also notes that the trailing newline is lost. This matches the known bug's mechanism and symptoms exactly.

". `TextWrapper.wrap()` returns an empty list for an empty or whitespace-only line, so those lines vanish from the output. With the default `replace_whitespace=True`, the trailing newline kept by `splitlines(True)` becomes a space and is dropped, so a trailing newline in the input is lost too. For example, `wordwrap("first

second
", 80)` returns "first
second" instead of "first

second
", which merges paragraphs in templates. The fix sets `replace_whitespace=False` and splits with `splitlines()` (no kept ends). It appends the original line whenever the wrapper returns nothing, and appends a final empty element when the text ends with "
".

findings.description:
The rewrite changes behaviour for blank lines and trailing newlines. Each line from splitlines(True) goes through TextWrapper.wrap, which turns the newline into a space and then drops it. A blank line such as the one in "a

b" therefore yields an empty list and disappears, so paragraph breaks are collapsed. A trailing newline is also lost, because the lines are joined with "
" and there is no final separator. The old implementation preserved both, so this is a regression for existing wordwrap users.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same faulty check, `"." in str(filter_expression.var)`, and the same mechanism. It says literals such as `{{ "a..b"|upper }}` wrongly trigger the deprecation warning and would become errors later. It also gives the same remedy: apply the check only to actual variable lookups. Finding 1 is about origin being None, which is a different issue.
ground_truth: The new deprecation check in `Parser.parse()` for variable nodes tests `".." in str(filter_expression.var)`. For constant expressions, `filter_expression.var` is the resolved literal value (a string or translated string), not a `Variable` lookup. So a template containing a literal with two consecutive dots, such as `{{ "a..b" }}` or `{{ 'a..b'|upper }}`, wrongly emits a `RemovedInDjango70Warning` about double-dot lookups. That warning becomes an exception when warnings are treated as errors. The check would also reject valid templates once it is elevated to an error as planned. The fix applies the check only when the expression is a variable lookup: `filter_expression.is_var and ".." in filter_expression.var.var`.

findings.description: The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals and ordinary text, not just variable lookups. For a literal such as `{{ "Wait..." }}`, `{{ "a..b"|upper }}` or `{{ _("loading...") }}`, `FilterExpression.var` is the literal string (or a Variable wrapping it), and its text contains `..`. These templates have no double-dot lookup, yet they now emit a RemovedInDjango70Warning. When the deprecation ends and the warning becomes an error, they would raise TemplateSyntaxError. The check should apply only to non-literal Variable lookups, such as the `lookups` of a Variable.

The warning message reads `self.origin.name` without a guard. `Parser.origin` can be None when a Parser is built directly, as some code and tests do, so a `..` in a variable raises AttributeError instead of a warning. Template compilation normally sets an origin, so this only affects direct Parser use.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same faulty check. It quotes `"." in str(filter_expression.var)` and explains that it "also matches string literals and translated literals, not just variable lookups." It notes that such templates emit a spurious RemovedInDjango70Warning and would later raise an error. Its suggested fix, applying the check only to real variable lookups, matches the known bug's fix.
ground_truth: The new deprecation check in `Parser.parse()` for variable nodes tests `".." in str(filter_expression.var)`. For constant expressions, `filter_expression.var` is the resolved literal value (a string or translated string), not a `Variable` lookup. So a template containing a literal with two consecutive dots, such as `{{ "a..b" }}` or `{{ 'a..b'|upper }}`, wrongly emits a `RemovedInDjango70Warning` about double-dot lookups. That warning becomes an exception when warnings are treated as errors. The check would also reject valid templates once it is elevated to an error as planned. The fix applies the check only when the expression is a variable lookup: `filter_expression.is_var and ".." in filter_expression.var.var`.

findings.description: The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals and translated literals, not just variable lookups. For `{{ "Loading..." }}` or `{{ _("Wait...") }}`, `FilterExpression.var` is the literal string or a Variable whose `str()` is the original text, and either contains `..`. These templates now emit a RemovedInDjango70Warning. Once the deprecation ends and the warning becomes an error, they would raise TemplateSyntaxError. The check should only apply to real variable lookups, for example when `var` is a Variable with `lookups` set and one of the lookups is empty.

justification: Finding 0 states that "Hard-coding the model's db_table as the alias is also wrong if the foreign-related field lives on a parent table (multi-table inheritance...)". It adds that "the old `field__in` lookup resolved the join and alias correctly in those cases." This is the known bug's mechanism: `ColPairs` pairs `queryset.model._meta.db_table` with `foreign_related_fields` without resolving them through the ORM, so under MTI the column ends up referenced on the wrong table. The finding's example (`to_field` on an inherited field) differs slightly from the known bug's (a `Restaurant` prefetch queryset for an FK to `Place`). The faulty code and failure mechanism are the same, and the finding would have led a maintainer to the actual bug.
ground_truth: `ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.get_prefetch_querysets()` now filters with `TupleIn(ColPairs(queryset.model._meta.db_table, related_fields, related_fields, self.field), ...)`, where `related_fields = self.field.foreign_related_fields`. Those are fields of the FK's target model, but the table alias comes from the prefetch queryset's model. With a custom prefetch queryset on a multi-table- inheritance subclass of the target, the two do not match. Example: a FK to `Place` prefetched with `Prefetch("place", queryset=Restaurant.objects.all())`. The generated SQL references the parent's column (e.g. `id`) on the child's table, which has no such column, so `prefetch_related` crashes with a database error. The old `field__in` kwarg filter resolved the field names through the ORM and did not have this problem. The fix resolves each field by name against the prefetch queryset (`queryset.query.resolve_ref(field.name).target`), so the columns match the queryset's model.

findings.description: The prefetch filter is now always a TupleIn over ColPairs keyed on queryset.model._meta.db_table, including the common single-column FK case. Single-column prefetches used to produce a plain `col IN (...)`. They now go through tuple-lookup SQL or its OR fallback, and None values in instances_dict keys are no longer dropped as In did. Hard-coding the model's db_table as the alias is also wrong if the foreign-related field lives on a parent table (multi-table inheritance, to_field on an inherited field) or the queryset uses a different alias. The old `field__in` lookup resolved the join and alias correctly in those cases. The result is a possible regression in SQL shape and correctness.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same faulty change. It says passing `writer="html"` makes docutils "treat the string as the writer object", which leads to an "AttributeError on `str`" and "breaks all admindocs RST rendering". That is the same mechanism as the known bug. The finding misses that docutils 0.22+ accepts string writer names, but it would still lead a maintainer to the actual defect on older docutils versions.
ground_truth: In `django/contrib/admindocs/utils.py`, `parse_rst()` was changed to call `docutils.core.publish_parts(..., writer="html", ...)` instead of `writer_name="html"`, to silence a deprecation warning in docutils 0.22+. Passing a string writer name through the `writer` parameter only works in docutils 0.22+. In docutils 0.19–0.21, `writer` must be a writer instance. With an older docutils installed, every admindocs reStructuredText rendering (docstrings for views, models, template tags, filters) therefore fails, typically with an AttributeError when docutils treats the string "html" as a writer object. The fix creates an instance with `docutils.writers.get_writer_class("html")()` and passes that as `writer`, which works across docutils 0.19 through 0.22.

findings.description: `docutils.core.publish_parts` has no string-valued `writer` argument. `writer` expects a Writer instance and `writer_name` is the string argument. Passing `writer="html"` makes docutils treat the string as the writer object, and `set_components` will not apply the default writer name. Later steps that use writer attributes such as `settings_spec`, `translate` and `parts` then fail with AttributeError on `str`. Also, `writer_name` falls back to the default `pseudoxml`, so even if the call did not crash, the output would not be HTML. This breaks all admindocs RST rendering.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug exactly. It says the check uses `self.fields`, which "keeps the raw '-' prefix", so a valid index like `Index(fields=['-name'])` produces a bogus E012 error, and it recommends using `fields_orders` instead. Findings 1 and 2 describe different issues: the per-database loop placement and duplicated feature warnings.
ground_truth: The new `Index.check()` method passes `{*self.fields, *self.include, *references}` to `model._check_local_fields()`. `self.fields` holds the raw field strings, including the "-" prefix used for descending order. The old Model-level check used the field names from `index.fields_orders`, which has that prefix stripped. As a result, a valid index such as `models.Index(fields=["-name"], name="idx")` now fails the system check with "'indexes' refers to the nonexistent field '-name'" (models.E012). The fix passes `field for field, _ in self.fields_orders` instead of `self.fields`.

findings.description: The field check uses `self.fields`, which keeps the raw '-' prefix for descending fields (e.g. '-name'). The original code used `fields_orders`, which strips it. A valid index like `Index(fields=['-name'])` now reports a bogus models.E012 error saying it refers to the nonexistent field '-name'. It should use the stripped field names from `fields_orders`.

The local-field check (E012, E013, E016 and similar) now runs inside the per-database loop in `_check_indexes`. If `databases` is empty or None, or the router disallows migration, these errors are never reported. With multiple databases they are reported once per database. Previously they ran once regardless of databases, which is why many tests had to be changed to pass `databases=`. Passing a set also makes the order of the resulting errors nondeterministic.

The feature-warning checks (W037, W040, W043) were moved into the per-index method but still scan all of `model._meta.indexes`. W037 even tests `self.condition` inside a generator over unrelated indexes. As a result, W040 and W043 are emitted for every index in the model if any one index uses the unsupported feature, even for indexes that don't use it. A model with N indexes produces N duplicate warnings instead of one, which is a behavior regression.

justification: The known bug is that `Index.check()` passes `self.fields`, which still carry the '-' prefix for descending order, so valid descending indexes fail with E012. Finding 0 is about checks being skipped when no database is given, or duplicated across databases. Finding 1 is about duplicate feature warnings and the misused loop variable in the W037 check. Neither mentions the '-' prefix or the switch from `fields_orders` to `self.fields`.
ground_truth: The new `Index.check()` method passes `{*self.fields, *self.include, *references}` to `model._check_local_fields()`. `self.fields` holds the raw field strings, including the "-" prefix used for descending order. The old Model-level check used the field names from `index.fields_orders`, which has that prefix stripped. As a result, a valid index such as `models.Index(fields=["-name"], name="idx")` now fails the system check with "'indexes' refers to the nonexistent field '-name'" (models.E012). The fix passes `field for field, _ in self.fields_orders` instead of `self.fields`.

findings.description: Index checks now run only inside the `for db in databases` loop, and only for databases that allow migrating the model. Name checks (E033/E034) and field checks (E012-style `indexes` errors) used to run unconditionally. With `Model.check()` and no databases, or a model that no database allows migrating, these errors are silently dropped. The existing tests had to be changed to pass `databases=` to keep passing. With several databases, the same name and field errors are reported once per database.

The feature warnings W037, W040 and W043 still scan `model._meta.indexes` (`any(index.include for index in model._meta.indexes)`). Now that `check()` runs once per index, every index on the model emits the warning if any one index uses the feature. A model with N indexes and one covering index gets N duplicate W040 warnings, and likewise for W043. W037 uses `self.condition` inside a generator over `index`, so it ignores the loop variable. This is a regression from the previous single warning per database.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect as the known bug. It notes that `window.relatedWindows` is undefined in production because the array is a module-local const. It says this causes a TypeError on `.indexOf` before `win.close()`, so the popup stays open. It also points out that the tests mask the problem by creating `window.relatedWindows` themselves.
ground_truth: In `RelatedObjectLookups.js`, the change rewrote `dismissRelatedLookupPopup` to use `window.relatedWindows.indexOf(win)` and `window.relatedWindows.splice(index, 1)` instead of the IIFE-local `relatedWindows` array. The module never assigns `relatedWindows` to `window`, so in a real admin page `window.relatedWindows` is undefined. Calling `.indexOf` on it throws a TypeError before `win.close()` runs. As a result, picking an object in a raw-id/related lookup popup sets the value but leaves the popup open. The new test hid the bug because it created `window.relatedWindows` itself. The fix went back to the module- local `relatedWindows`, exported it as `window.relatedWindows = relatedWindows`, and removed the test's own initialization.

findings.description: The code now reads `window.relatedWindows`, but the file declares `relatedWindows` as a block-scoped `const` (`const relatedWindows = []`). It is not a property of `window`, and `showRelatedObjectPopup` pushes windows onto the local const. In production `window.relatedWindows` is undefined. `dismissRelatedLookupPopup` therefore throws a TypeError on `.indexOf`, after the value is set but before `win.close()`. Raw-id lookup popups would no longer close or clean up. The new tests only pass because they create `window.relatedWindows` themselves. The fix should have kept using the local `relatedWindows` or exposed it deliberately.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect. It says `relatedWindows` is IIFE-local and never exported, so `window.relatedWindows` is undefined. It notes that `.indexOf` throws a TypeError before `win.close()`, leaving the popup open. It also points out that the test masks the problem by initializing `window.relatedWindows` itself.
ground_truth: In `RelatedObjectLookups.js`, the change rewrote `dismissRelatedLookupPopup` to use `window.relatedWindows.indexOf(win)` and `window.relatedWindows.splice(index, 1)` instead of the IIFE-local `relatedWindows` array. The module never assigns `relatedWindows` to `window`, so in a real admin page `window.relatedWindows` is undefined. Calling `.indexOf` on it throws a TypeError before `win.close()` runs. As a result, picking an object in a raw-id/related lookup popup sets the value but leaves the popup open. The new test hid the bug because it created `window.relatedWindows` itself. The fix went back to the module- local `relatedWindows`, exported it as `window.relatedWindows = relatedWindows`, and removed the test's own initialization.

findings.description: `relatedWindows` is a local `const` inside the IIFE in RelatedObjectLookups.js and is never exported to `window`. Changing it to `window.relatedWindows` makes `window.relatedWindows` undefined in real admin pages. The next call to `dismissRelatedLookupPopup` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'indexOf')`. This happens after the value is set but before `win.close()`, so the popup never closes and the window is never removed from the real tracking array. The new test hides this by setting `window.relatedWindows = window.relatedWindows || []` in `beforeEach`. The original unqualified reference is correct and should be restored.

justification: Finding 0 is about duplicate appending of db_default fields that are already in returning_fields. The known bug is a different mechanism: the `elif field.db_returning: returning_fields.remove(field)` branch drops db_returning fields with explicitly set values, even on backends that support RETURNING. That leaves stale in-memory values on the instance. The finding does not mention this removal behavior.
ground_truth: In the insert branch of `Model._save_table`, the change builds `returning_fields = list(meta.db_returning_fields)` and then, for each insert field, calls `returning_fields.remove(field)` (the `elif field.db_returning:` branch) whenever the field's pre_save value is not an expression. Before this change, every `db_returning` field was always fetched back via RETURNING and assigned to the instance. Now a `db_returning` field with an explicitly set value keeps the in-memory Python value instead of the value the database actually stored. This happens even on backends that support RETURNING (PostgreSQL, SQLite, Oracle). For example, an explicitly set primary key or a custom `db_returning=True` field whose stored or converted value (via `from_db_value`, normalization or triggers) differs from the assigned value is left stale on the instance after `save()`/`create()`. The fix only removes such fields from `returning_fields` when the backend cannot return columns from insert, and never removes the auto field when the pk was set.

findings.description: In the insert path, `returning_fields` starts as `list(meta.db_returning_fields)`. A field that is already in it (a `db_default` field on backends that support RETURNING) is appended again when its value has `resolve_expression`. That always holds for the `DatabaseDefault` placeholder, and also when the user assigns an expression. The field then appears twice in the RETURNING clause and in `returning_fields`. The returned columns no longer line up with the intended fields, and `_assign_returned_values` assigns the wrong values or does so redundantly. This is a regression for every model with a `db_default` on SQLite, PostgreSQL and Oracle. An `if field not in returning_fields` guard is missing.

justification: Finding 0 is about the expression branch of the insert loop. It says a db_returning field holding an expression gets appended to `returning_fields` a second time, so the RETURNING clause has duplicate columns. The known bug is in the `elif field.db_returning: returning_fields.remove(field)` branch. That branch drops db_returning fields with explicit values, which leaves stale in-memory values on the instance. These are different defects.
ground_truth: In the insert branch of `Model._save_table`, the change builds `returning_fields = list(meta.db_returning_fields)` and then, for each insert field, calls `returning_fields.remove(field)` (the `elif field.db_returning:` branch) whenever the field's pre_save value is not an expression. Before this change, every `db_returning` field was always fetched back via RETURNING and assigned to the instance. Now a `db_returning` field with an explicitly set value keeps the in-memory Python value instead of the value the database actually stored. This happens even on backends that support RETURNING (PostgreSQL, SQLite, Oracle). For example, an explicitly set primary key or a custom `db_returning=True` field whose stored or converted value (via `from_db_value`, normalization or triggers) differs from the assigned value is left stale on the instance after `save()`/`create()`. The fix only removes such fields from `returning_fields` when the backend cannot return columns from insert, and never removes the auto field when the pk was set.

findings.description: In the insert path, a field that is already in `meta.db_returning_fields` is appended to `returning_fields` again whenever its value has `resolve_expression`. A field with a `db_default` is the main case, because its attribute holds a `DatabaseDefault` expression and `field.db_returning` is true. The upstream version guards this with `if field not in returning_fields`, but this diff does not. The field then appears twice in the RETURNING clause, producing duplicate columns. `_assign_returned_values` zips the returned values against the longer list, so the field is assigned twice and the returned columns no longer line up with `returning_fields`.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect as the known bug. It says the function "now raises ValueError for over-long codes" and that "Existing callers only catch LookupError". It also says long cookies or URL prefixes would make LocaleMiddleware or get_language_from_request "raise an uncaught ValueError and return a 500". That is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism.
ground_truth: The security patch added a length check to `get_supported_language_variant()`. When `lang_code` exceeds `LANGUAGE_CODE_MAX_LENGTH` (500) and no generic variant can be cut off (or `strict=True`), it raises `ValueError("'lang_code' exceeds the maximum accepted length")`. This breaks the function's documented contract of raising `LookupError` when nothing is found. Callers like `LocaleMiddleware` and `get_language_from_path()`/`get_language_from_request()` only catch `LookupError`, and with the default strict=False a long code without a usable "-" still reaches the `ValueError` branch. So a request whose URL language prefix or language cookie is longer than 500 characters crashes with an unhandled ValueError (HTTP 500) instead of falling back to another language. Fixed by raising `LookupError(lang_code)` instead of ValueError.

findings.description: get_supported_language_variant() now raises ValueError for over-long codes (strict=True, or non-strict with no hyphen). Existing callers only catch LookupError. get_language_from_request() reads the language cookie and passes it in without a length check. get_language_from_path() passes a regex-matched path segment with strict=True, and that regex has no length limit. A request with a cookie or URL prefix longer than 500 characters (for example 'xxxx…') would therefore make LocaleMiddleware or get_language_from_request raise an uncaught ValueError and return a 500, where it previously fell back to the default language or a 404.

justification: Finding [0] says the UNNEST path ignores custom `field.get_placeholder()` logic and that adapter-wrapped values may fail to cast. It does not mention that `db_type` includes length/precision parameters such as `varchar(50)`. It also does not say that an explicit cast to those types silently truncates strings or rounds decimals. That is a different defect from the known bug.
ground_truth: The new `SQLInsertCompiler.assemble_as_sql` in the PostgreSQL compiler builds each UNNEST placeholder as `(%s)::<db_type>[]`, where `db_type` comes from `field.db_type(self.connection)`. That type string includes the column's parameters, e.g. `varchar(50)` or `numeric(5, 2)`. In PostgreSQL an explicit cast to a length- limited type silently truncates or rounds values instead of raising an error. So `bulk_create()` of two or more objects whose CharField value exceeds `max_length` silently inserts a truncated string, where the regular VALUES insert would fail with a "value too long" error. The same applies to rounding of decimals. The fix strips the parameters from the type (`db_type.split("(")[0]`), so the cast is to e.g. `varchar[]` and the column's own constraints apply on insert.

findings.description: The UNNEST path builds placeholders as a plain `(%s)::<db_type>[]` for every field. It ignores any custom `field.get_placeholder()` or `get_db_prep_save()` placeholder logic that the base `assemble_as_sql` applies. Fields that rely on such placeholders (for example GIS geometry fields, or custom fields with their own placeholder) get a bare cast instead of their custom SQL. Values that cannot be cast through an array literal, such as adapter-wrapped values, can also make a previously working multi-row `bulk_create()` fail on PostgreSQL. Only arrays and `as_sql` values are excluded from the optimization.

justification: The known bug is about casting to parameterized types like varchar(50)[], which silently truncates or rounds values. Finding [0] is about a different defect: the UNNEST path skips the per-field get_placeholder wrappers used by PostGIS. It does not mention truncation or type parameters, so it does not match.
ground_truth: The new `SQLInsertCompiler.assemble_as_sql` in the PostgreSQL compiler builds each UNNEST placeholder as `(%s)::<db_type>[]`, where `db_type` comes from `field.db_type(self.connection)`. That type string includes the column's parameters, e.g. `varchar(50)` or `numeric(5, 2)`. In PostgreSQL an explicit cast to a length- limited type silently truncates or rounds values instead of raising an error. So `bulk_create()` of two or more objects whose CharField value exceeds `max_length` silently inserts a truncated string, where the regular VALUES insert would fail with a "value too long" error. The same applies to rounding of decimals. The fix strips the parameters from the type (`db_type.split("(")[0]`), so the cast is to e.g. `varchar[]` and the column's own constraints apply on insert.

findings.description: The UNNEST path skips the per-field placeholders that the base assemble_as_sql applies via get_placeholder(). A field that defines get_placeholder, such as PostGIS geometry fields, normally wraps its value in a SQL function like ST_GeomFromEWKB(%s). Here the value is cast straight to db_type[] instead. Because PostGIS operations inherit from the PostgreSQL operations and so pick up this compiler, bulk_create with two or more rows can generate wrong or failing SQL. The condition at line 31 only excludes compilable values and array fields, and does not check for custom placeholders.

justification: The known bug is a pickling failure: the namedtuple's typename "Attachment" does not match its module attribute name "EmailAttachment". Finding [0] instead says attachments passed to the constructor are not converted to named tuples. That is a different issue, and it does not mention pickling or the typename/qualname mismatch.
ground_truth: The change adds the module-level `EmailAttachment = namedtuple("Attachment", ["filename", "content", "mimetype"])` in `django/core/mail/message.py`. `EmailMessage.attach()` now stores each attachment as an instance of it. Pickle serializes namedtuple instances by looking up the class by its `__qualname__` ("Attachment") in its module. No `Attachment` attribute exists in `django.core.mail.message`; the class is bound to the name `EmailAttachment`. As a result, pickling an `EmailMessage` with any attachment fails with a `PicklingError` (attribute lookup Attachment on django.core.mail.message failed), e.g. `msg.attach("a.txt", "x", "text/plain"); pickle.dumps(msg)`, which breaks queuing emails through task queues or caches. The fix renames the namedtuple type names to match their variable names (`namedtuple("EmailAttachment", ...)`, and likewise `EmailAlternative`).

findings.description: Only attachments added through attach() become EmailAttachment named tuples. Attachments passed to the EmailMessage constructor (attachments=[(filename, content, mimetype)]) are not converted, so they stay plain tuples. Code that accesses msg.attachments[i].filename or .content then raises AttributeError for constructor-supplied attachments, which contradicts the new docs. A 2-tuple passed to the constructor also stays a 2-tuple, so the attributes are inconsistent. The constructor should route attachments through attach().

justification: Finding 1 identifies the same defect. It says the namedtuple typename is "Attachment" while the module-level name is `EmailAttachment`, so pickling fails because pickle looks up `django.core.mail.message.Attachment`, which does not exist. That is exactly the known bug. Finding 0 is about backward compatibility with plain tuples, which is a different issue.
ground_truth: The change adds the module-level `EmailAttachment = namedtuple("Attachment", ["filename", "content", "mimetype"])` in `django/core/mail/message.py`. `EmailMessage.attach()` now stores each attachment as an instance of it. Pickle serializes namedtuple instances by looking up the class by its `__qualname__` ("Attachment") in its module. No `Attachment` attribute exists in `django.core.mail.message`; the class is bound to the name `EmailAttachment`. As a result, pickling an `EmailMessage` with any attachment fails with a `PicklingError` (attribute lookup Attachment on django.core.mail.message failed), e.g. `msg.attach("a.txt", "x", "text/plain"); pickle.dumps(msg)`, which breaks queuing emails through task queues or caches. The fix renames the namedtuple type names to match their variable names (`namedtuple("EmailAttachment", ...)`, and likewise `EmailAlternative`).

findings.description: _create_alternatives now reads `alternative.content` and `alternative.mimetype`. Existing code that appends plain tuples to `msg.alternatives`, or assigns a list of tuples to it after construction, previously worked. It now raises AttributeError when the message is built, because plain tuples have no such attributes. This breaks backward compatibility. The old code unpacked positionally with `*alternative`.

The namedtuple typename is "Attachment" but the module-level name is `EmailAttachment`. Pickling or deepcopying an EmailMessage that has attachments fails, because pickle looks up `django.core.mail.message.Attachment`, which does not exist. Plain tuples pickled fine before, so this is a regression for anyone who pickles messages, for example when queueing them.

justification: Finding 0 describes both parts of the known bug. It says that removing `single_object` causes a `TypeError` for existing callers ("Any caller that already passes `single_object=True` ... will now get a `TypeError`"). It also says the return type now depends on input length, so a one-item queryset returns a single instance rather than a list.
ground_truth: The change removed the keyword-only `single_object` parameter from `LogEntryManager.log_actions()` and replaced the `if single_object and log_entry_list` check with `if len(log_entry_list) == 1`, which returns the bare saved instance. This breaks the public API released in Django 5.1 in two ways. First, third-party code calling `LogEntry.objects.log_actions(..., single_object=True)` now fails with `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'single_object'` after a point-release upgrade. Second, callers passing a multi-object queryset that happens to contain exactly one object now get a single `LogEntry` instance instead of a list, so code that iterates or indexes the result breaks. The fix restores the `single_object=False` keyword argument and passes it from `log_addition`/`log_change`. It keeps saving one-element lists via `save()` so signals still fire, but returns `[instance]` unless `single_object` is true.

findings.description: The keyword-only `single_object` parameter is removed from the public `LogEntryManager.log_actions()`. Any caller that already passes `single_object=True` (the parameter existed in released 5.1 versions) will now get a `TypeError`. That is a compatibility break in a patch-release regression fix. Also, the return type now depends on the length of the input: a single `LogEntry` instance for one object, a list for any other count. A one-item queryset therefore behaves differently from an N-item one.

justification: Finding 0 is about a TypeError in the form field path when max_length=None, from comparing `len(ip_str) > None`. The known bug is a different defect. There, `is_valid_ipv6_address` receives non-string inputs such as IPv6Address instances or ints, `len()` fails on them, and the resulting TypeError is not caught. The faulty input and the call path both differ, so the finding does not match.
ground_truth: The change makes `is_valid_ipv6_address()` call the new helper `_ipv6_address_from_str()` instead of `ipaddress.IPv6Address(ip_str)`. The helper begins with `if len(ip_str) > max_length`, and `is_valid_ipv6_address()` still only catches `ValueError`. Before, non-string values that `ipaddress.IPv6Address` accepts, such as an `ipaddress.IPv6Address` instance or an int, were handled. Now they raise an uncaught `TypeError` (e.g. "object of type 'IPv6Address' has no len()"). As a result, `validate_ipv6_address(ipaddress.IPv6Address('::1'))` and `validate_ipv46_address(...)` crash instead of validating or raising `ValidationError`. The fix returns True early for `ipaddress.IPv6Address` instances and catches `TypeError` as well as `ValueError`, returning False.

findings.description: The form field passes `max_length=self.max_length` into `clean_ipv6_address`. `kwargs.setdefault` does not replace an explicit `max_length=None`, so a caller who sets that to remove the length limit leaves `self.max_length` as None. Any IPv6 value containing ':' then reaches `len(ip_str) > None` in `_ipv6_address_from_str`, which raises TypeError (a 500 error) instead of validating or returning a ValidationError. This is a regression for existing code that passes `max_length=None`.

justification: Finding 0 points at the same faulty guard. It says the guard checks `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` instead of the target select, so for a plain select "`SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, ...)` dereferences an undefined `SelectBox.cache[select.id]` and throws a TypeError." That is the same mechanism as the known bug. The finding names a different consequence (remaining selects are not updated) rather than the popup failing to close, but it would have led a maintainer to the actual fix of checking `SelectBox.cache[select.id]`.
ground_truth: The change added a block to `updateRelatedSelectsOptions` in RelatedObjectLookups.js that, after appending a new option to another related select, calls `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, option)` and `SelectBox.redisplay(select.id)`. The guard is only `window.SelectBox !== undefined && !SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]`; it never checks that `select` itself is managed by SelectBox. Consider a form with several relations to the same model where only some use `filter_horizontal`, so SelectBox.js is loaded. Adding an object via the '+' popup then reaches other plain `<select>` widgets that have no `SelectBox.cache` entry. `add_to_cache` then pushes onto an undefined cache entry and throws a TypeError. That aborts `dismissAddRelatedObjectPopup`, so the popup window never closes. The fix adds the condition `SelectBox.cache[select.id]`, so the cache is updated only for fields SelectBox actually manages.

findings.description: The SelectBox cache guard tests `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` but then updates the cache for `select.id`. The guard should be about the target select. If a popup is added from a plain FK select, `currentSelect` has no cache entry, so the guard is true for every other related select. For a plain FK select that is also an `available-source` target, `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, ...)` dereferences an undefined `SelectBox.cache[select.id]` and throws a TypeError. That aborts the forEach, so the remaining selects are not updated. In the opposite case, an add from the m2m popup passes `toElem`, whose cache exists, so the guard is false and the filter-widget cache is never updated for other m2m widgets. They will show the new option until they redisplay, and then it disappears.

justification: Finding 0 points to the same faulty guard at line 113. It explains that when the condition is true, `add_to_cache` runs for `select.id`: "If `select.id` has no cache entry either, that call throws a TypeError. The guard should check `select.id`." This is the same mechanism as the known bug: a missing check that `select` is managed by SelectBox causes a TypeError on an undefined cache entry. The fix it proposes also matches. The finding does not mention the popup failing to close, but it identifies the same defect.
ground_truth: The change added a block to `updateRelatedSelectsOptions` in RelatedObjectLookups.js that, after appending a new option to another related select, calls `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, option)` and `SelectBox.redisplay(select.id)`. The guard is only `window.SelectBox !== undefined && !SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]`; it never checks that `select` itself is managed by SelectBox. Consider a form with several relations to the same model where only some use `filter_horizontal`, so SelectBox.js is loaded. Adding an object via the '+' popup then reaches other plain `<select>` widgets that have no `SelectBox.cache` entry. `add_to_cache` then pushes onto an undefined cache entry and throws a TypeError. That aborts `dismissAddRelatedObjectPopup`, so the popup window never closes. The fix adds the condition `SelectBox.cache[select.id]`, so the cache is updated only for fields SelectBox actually manages.

findings.description: The cache guard checks `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` but the cache update targets `select.id`. When the change comes from an M2M "+" popup, `currentSelect` is the `_to` box, which always has a cache entry, so the condition is false. The new option is therefore never added to the SelectBox cache of other related filter-horizontal "from" boxes. Those boxes show it in the DOM, but a later `redisplay`, filter or move operation drops it or fails to move it. When `currentSelect` is a plain select with no cache entry, the condition is true and `add_to_cache` runs for `select.id`. If `select.id` has no cache entry either, that call throws a TypeError. The guard should check `select.id`.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says `% self.min_length` is applied to the msgids before the ngettext lookup, so the formatted strings no longer match the catalog entries. It states the consequence: "Users with a non-English language will see the English message." It also notes the dropped params.
ground_truth: The new `MinimumLengthValidator.get_error_message()` applies `% self.min_length` to each string literal before passing it to `ngettext`. The msgids that `ngettext` receives are therefore already formatted strings, such as "This password is too short. It must contain at least 8 characters.". These never match the translation catalog entries, which contain the `%d` placeholder. As a result, with a non-English active language (e.g. French), the too-short password error is always shown untranslated in English. The fix calls `ngettext` with the unformatted singular/plural msgids and applies `% self.min_length` to the translated result. It also restores `params={"min_length": ...}` on the raised `ValidationError`.

findings.description: MinimumLengthValidator.get_error_message() applies `% self.min_length` to the ngettext msgids before translation lookup. The lookup keys become literal strings such as "...at least 8 characters." instead of the catalog's "...%(min_length)d character(s).", so existing translations no longer match. Users with a non-English language will see the English message. The `min_length` entry in ValidationError params was also dropped, which regresses existing behavior for code that reads `params`.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It states that min_length is interpolated into the msgid before ngettext is called, so the lookup uses strings like "...at least 8 characters." that are in no catalog, and the error "is therefore never translated and always appears in English". It also notes that params are dropped. Both points match the known bug and its fix.
ground_truth: The new `MinimumLengthValidator.get_error_message()` applies `% self.min_length` to each string literal before passing it to `ngettext`. The msgids that `ngettext` receives are therefore already formatted strings, such as "This password is too short. It must contain at least 8 characters.". These never match the translation catalog entries, which contain the `%d` placeholder. As a result, with a non-English active language (e.g. French), the too-short password error is always shown untranslated in English. The fix calls `ngettext` with the unformatted singular/plural msgids and applies `% self.min_length` to the translated result. It also restores `params={"min_length": ...}` on the raised `ValidationError`.

findings.description: MinimumLengthValidator now interpolates min_length into the msgid before calling ngettext ("... %d character." % self.min_length). The gettext lookup therefore uses strings such as "...at least 8 characters.", which are not in any translation catalog. The existing catalogs use the msgid with %(min_length)d, and the string extractor sees a different, non-literal msgid. The too-short error is therefore never translated and always appears in English, a regression for non-English users. The change also drops params={"min_length": ...} from the ValidationError, so code that inspects error.params loses the value.

justification: Finding 2 identifies the same defect: "The operation ignores the target database alias. `Permission.objects.filter` and `permission.save()` do not use `using=db`, and the ContentType queryset is not bound to the alias either. With multiple databases, migrating a non-default database reads and writes the wrong one." This is the same faulty code and failure mechanism as the known bug. The other findings describe different issues: substring matching, custom permissions, the swallowed IntegrityError, and operation ordering.
ground_truth: In the new `RenamePermission._rename`, the code reads `db = schema_editor.connection.alias` but never applies it to the lookups. `ContentType.objects.filter(...)` and `Permission.objects.filter(content_type_id__in=...)` therefore run against the default (router-chosen) database rather than the one being migrated. Running `migrate --database=other` on an app with a `RenameModel` reads and renames permissions in the default database, or finds nothing there. Meanwhile the permissions in the database actually being migrated keep their old codenames and names. The fix adds `.using(db)` to both the ContentType and Permission querysets so the operation works on the migration's database connection.

findings.description: The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, which is a substring match. Renaming `Order` would also match content types such as `orderitem` or `preorder` in the same app. Permissions of unrelated models would then be renamed to `*_neworder`, and the match should be exact.

Every permission on the matching content types is rewritten to `<prefix>_<newmodel>` with a default name, where the prefix is `codename.split('_')[0]`. Custom permissions (for example `can_export_oldmodel`, or any with a custom name or verbose_name) are collapsed into `can_newmodel` or overwritten. Custom permission names are lost, and several custom permissions can collide with each other. Only the four default permissions should be renamed.

The operation ignores the target database alias. `Permission.objects.filter` and `permission.save()` do not use `using=db`, and the ContentType queryset is not bound to the alias either. With multiple databases, migrating a non-default database reads and writes the wrong one. The router may also direct the writes elsewhere.

`IntegrityError` is silently swallowed on a codename conflict. The old permission is left behind and still points at the old codename, with no warning. Users who hold that permission keep it under a stale codename instead of the renamed one.

The auth handler inserts `RenamePermission` directly after `RenameModel`, which puts it before the `RenameContentType` operation that contenttypes inserted. Backward migration runs operations in reverse, so `RenameContentType` reverts first. The content type then already has the old model name, but `rename_backward` filters on the new model name, so it can match nothing and permissions would not be restored.

justification: The known bug is that the ContentType and Permission querysets do not use `.using(db)`, so they hit the wrong database. Finding 0 is about the `icontains` substring match. Finding 1 is about the prefix-splitting corrupting custom permissions. Neither mentions the unused `db` alias or the multi-database problem.
ground_truth: In the new `RenamePermission._rename`, the code reads `db = schema_editor.connection.alias` but never applies it to the lookups. `ContentType.objects.filter(...)` and `Permission.objects.filter(content_type_id__in=...)` therefore run against the default (router-chosen) database rather than the one being migrated. Running `migrate --database=other` on an app with a `RenameModel` reads and renames permissions in the default database, or finds nothing there. Meanwhile the permissions in the database actually being migrated keep their old codenames and names. The fix adds `.using(db)` to both the ContentType and Permission querysets so the operation works on the migration's database connection.

findings.description: The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, which is a substring match rather than an exact match. Renaming `User` to `Member` also matches content types such as `userprofile` and `superuser`. All permissions on those unrelated models are then renamed to `*_member`, corrupting their codenames and names. The lookup should be `model=old_model.lower()`.

Every permission on the content type is rewritten using `codename.split('_')[0]` as the prefix. A custom permission like `can_publish_article` becomes `can_newmodel` with the name 'Can can new model'. Several custom permissions on one model collapse to the same codename, so only the first rename succeeds and the rest are silently dropped by the IntegrityError handler. Custom permissions are therefore lost or corrupted. The new name also ignores the model's `verbose_name`, overwriting any customized permission names.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It says the loop adds a name "if any class in the MRO defines it as a property" and that it "ignores whether a more-derived class overrides that name with a non-property". It also names the same consumers (`Model.__init__` and `_extract_model_params`) and proposes the same fix of tracking names already seen in more-derived classes.
ground_truth: The rewritten `Options._property_names` iterates over `self.model.__mro__` and adds every name whose value in some `klass.__dict__` is a `property`. It does not check whether a class earlier in the MRO already shadows that name with a non-property attribute. Example: an abstract parent model defines `foo` as a `@property` and a child model overrides `foo` with a plain attribute or a field. `foo` is still reported in the child's `_property_names`. Code that relies on this set then treats the name as a property and mishandles it, for example `Model.__init__`/`_prepare_related_fields` kwargs handling and `QuerySet` create/update_or_create validation. The old `inspect.getattr_static` version resolved the attribute as normal lookup would. The fix tracks names already seen in earlier MRO classes and only counts a property if its name was not defined in a more-derived class.

findings.description: The MRO loop collects a name if any class in the MRO defines it as a property. It ignores whether a more-derived class overrides that name with a non-property, such as a model field, a plain attribute or a method. The old `inspect.getattr_static` lookup returned only the most-derived attribute, so those names were excluded. Now a name like `foo` can appear in `_property_names` even though `Child.foo` is a field or a regular attribute. `Model.__init__` and `_extract_model_params` use this set to treat kwargs as property setters, so they can call `setattr` on the wrong thing or skip field validation. This is a regression. The fix is to track names already seen in more-derived classes and skip them.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect. It says the MRO loop "adds every property found in any class's __dict__ and never checks whether a more-derived class overrides that name with a non-property". It cites the same examples and affected code, Model.__init__ and get_or_create/update_or_create, and proposes the same fix of tracking names already seen.
ground_truth: The rewritten `Options._property_names` iterates over `self.model.__mro__` and adds every name whose value in some `klass.__dict__` is a `property`. It does not check whether a class earlier in the MRO already shadows that name with a non-property attribute. Example: an abstract parent model defines `foo` as a `@property` and a child model overrides `foo` with a plain attribute or a field. `foo` is still reported in the child's `_property_names`. Code that relies on this set then treats the name as a property and mishandles it, for example `Model.__init__`/`_prepare_related_fields` kwargs handling and `QuerySet` create/update_or_create validation. The old `inspect.getattr_static` version resolved the attribute as normal lookup would. The fix tracks names already seen in earlier MRO classes and only counts a property if its name was not defined in a more-derived class.

findings.description: The new MRO loop adds every property found in any class's __dict__ and never checks whether a more-derived class overrides that name with a non-property. The old getattr_static approach resolved the name to the first MRO match, so it did not report such names. For example, a subclass (or abstract-base child) can replace an inherited property with a model field or plain attribute. That name is still reported as a property here. This affects Model.__init__, which treats property names as settable kwargs, and the get_or_create/update_or_create defaults handling. It also affects the pk-property check. The fix is to track names already seen in more-derived classes and skip them.

justification: Finding 0 notes that the NotSupportedError guard is bypassed when `Subquery.resolve_expression` returns an `ExpressionWrapper`, "when an explicit `output_field` differs from the query's own". It treats this as a narrow edge case where the field genuinely differs. It never identifies the actual defect: `self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field` uses `Field.__eq__` (creation_counter/model), so separately instantiated fields of the same type always compare unequal and are always wrapped. The finding accepts the comparison logic as correct and complains about a different gap in the guard.
ground_truth: The new `Subquery.resolve_expression()` is meant to drop the Subquery shim and return the bare resolved `Query`. It is supposed to wrap the query in an `ExpressionWrapper` only when the user passed an `output_field` that differs from the query's own. It tests this with `self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field`, but `Field.__eq__` compares fields by `creation_counter` and model, not by kind. So a separately instantiated field such as `IntegerField()` never equals the query's model field. As a result, any `Subquery(..., output_field=X())` is always wrapped in an `ExpressionWrapper`, even when `X` is the same field type as the selected column. Lookups that introspect the right-hand side as a `Query` then no longer recognize it, defeating the purpose of the change. One example is the tuple lookups' `isinstance(self.rhs, Query)` check, which is supposed to raise `NotSupportedError` for composite-pk comparisons against subqueries. The fix compares field types (`type(self.output_field) is not type(resolved.query.output_field)`) instead of using field equality.

findings.description: The NotSupportedError guard only fires when `self.rhs` is a bare `Query`. `Subquery.resolve_expression` returns `ExpressionWrapper(resolved.query, ...)` when an explicit `output_field` differs from the query's own, so `pk__gt=Subquery(..., output_field=...)` bypasses the check. On Oracle it then produces unsupported tuple-vs-subquery SQL and fails with a database error instead of the intended NotSupportedError. This is a narrow edge case.
